overview.title: Naming models and layers; declaring the input shape with keras.Input
overview.section: 7.2 Different ways to build Keras models
overview.main_topic: Giving explicit names to models and layers via the name argument, and making a Sequential model build on the fly by declaring keras.Input(shape=...) first.
overview.central_idea: Every Keras model and layer can be named; and if you add a keras.Input with the per-sample shape at the start of a Sequential model, it is built immediately, so you can call summary() after each add() to watch shapes evolve.
overview.importance: Readable names make summaries, saved weights and debugging far easier, and declaring the input up front removes the 'model not built' trap from p.217 — it also previews how the Functional API starts every model with an Input (p.219).
learning_objectives: Use the name argument on keras.Sequential and on layers.
Explain why you cannot call summary() before the model is built.
Declare an input shape in advance with keras.Input(shape=(3,)).
Distinguish the per-sample shape passed to Input from the batch shape passed to build().

summary:
The page continues the Sequential-model walkthrough with two practical tools.

**1. Naming.** The summary on p.217 showed an auto-generated name, `sequential_1`. In Keras you can name *everything* — every model, every layer — with the `name` argument. **Listing 7.6** creates `keras.Sequential(name="my_example_model")`, adds `Dense(64, activation="relu", name="my_first_layer")` and `Dense(10, activation="softmax", name="my_last_layer")`, builds it with `model.build((None, 3))` and prints a summary. The table is identical to Listing 7.5 (256 + 650 = 906 parameters, 3.54 KB) except that the model and layers now carry the chosen names.

**2. Declaring the input shape in advance.** When building incrementally, you'd like to print a summary after each `add()` — but a summary needs a built model. The fix is to tell the model its input shape up front with the **`Input` class**. **Listing 7.7** does `model.add(keras.Input(shape=(3,)))` before adding `Dense(64, activation="relu")`. The callout stresses that `shape` must be **the shape of each sample, not the shape of one batch** — so `(3,)`, not `(None, 3)` as in `build()`.

Because the input shape is known, each added layer is built immediately, and `summary()` works at any point. The output shown, for model `"sequential_2"`, lists just `dense_4 (Dense)` with output `(None, 64)` and 256 parameters (`Total params: 256 (1.00 KB)`). The next page (p.219) continues by adding the 10-unit layer and noting that this is a common debugging workflow for layers that transform shapes in complex ways, such as the convolutional layers of chapter 8.

paragraphs.excerpt: As you can see, your model happens to be named sequential_1.
paragraphs.what_it_says: The model in Listing 7.5 was auto-named sequential_1; you can give names to every model and every layer.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Without a name, Keras generates one from the class name plus a global counter (sequential, sequential_1, dense_2, ...). Supplying name= replaces this with something meaningful.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Meaningful names make summaries readable, help you find layers with model.get_layer(name), and make weight paths in saved files understandable.

concepts.name: keras.Input
concepts.definition: An object declaring the shape (per sample) and dtype of a model's input.
concepts.intuition: A labelled placeholder: 'samples of 3 numbers will arrive here'.
concepts.technical: keras.Input(shape=(3,)) yields a symbolic tensor of shape (None, 3); the batch axis is added automatically.
concepts.significance: Makes Sequential models build immediately, and is the starting point of every Functional model.
concepts.misconception: Passing the batch shape, e.g. shape=(None, 3) or shape=(32, 3); the shape must be that of one sample.

concepts.name: Naming models and layers
concepts.definition: Every Keras model and layer accepts a name argument.
concepts.intuition: Labels on boxes instead of 'box_1, box_2'.
concepts.technical: Unnamed objects get class-based names with global counters (sequential_2, dense_4).
concepts.significance: Clearer summaries, easier layer retrieval and debugging.
concepts.misconception: That names affect computation; they are purely identifiers.

concepts.name: Deferred weight creation
concepts.definition: Layers create weights once their input shape is known.
concepts.intuition: With an Input declared, the shape is known from the start, so building is no longer deferred.
concepts.technical: summary() needs a built model; an Input at the start lets each add() build its layer.
concepts.significance: Explains why Listing 7.7 can print a summary without build().
concepts.example: dense_4 shows 256 parameters right after it is added.
concepts.misconception: That you always need to call build() manually.

deeper.title: Two ways to state the input shape: build() vs Input
deeper.body:
From the book: `model.build((None, 3))` (Listing 7.6) and `keras.Input(shape=(3,))` (Listing 7.7) both fix the input size to 3 features. Beyond the book, the practical differences:

| | `build()` | `keras.Input` |
|---|---|---|
| Shape given | full batch shape `(None, 3)` | per-sample shape `(3,)` |
| When | after all layers are added | before the first layer |
| Summary after each `add()` | no | yes |

The Input approach is also exactly how Functional models begin (p.219).

deeper.title: Shape-checking as you build
deeper.body: Beyond the book: with an Input declared, a quick habit is `model.add(layer); print(model.output_shape)` after each line. Mismatches (e.g. forgetting to flatten an image before a Dense layer) show up immediately, not at `fit()` time.

visualizations.title: Listing 7.7 so far
visualizations.why: The model of Listing 7.7: Input of shape (3,) then Dense(64, relu), matching the one-row summary with 256 parameters.

misconceptions.claim: keras.Input(shape=(None, 3)) declares 3-feature inputs with any batch size.
misconceptions.correction: Input's shape is per sample: use shape=(3,). The batch axis is added automatically. (build() is different: it takes the full shape (None, 3).)

misconceptions.claim: Naming a layer changes its behaviour.
misconceptions.correction: Names are only identifiers; Listing 7.6's summary has the same shapes and 906 parameters as Listing 7.5.

misconceptions.claim: The Input counts as a layer with parameters.
misconceptions.correction: The summary shows only dense_4; the Input contributes no weights.

earlier.note: build(), model.weights and the auto-named summary of sequential_1.

later.note: The shape-debugging workflow continues, then the Functional API, which starts from an Input.

takeaways: Every Keras model and layer can be given a name via name=.
Adding keras.Input(shape=...) first makes a Sequential model build as you add layers.
Input's shape is per sample (3,), not per batch.
Use summary() after each add() to track output shapes.

questions.question: Which call correctly declares that each sample is a vector of 3 features in a Sequential model?
questions.explanation: The callout says shape must be the shape of each sample, not of a batch. (None, 3) and (32, 3) include a batch axis; batch=3 is not the right argument.

questions.question: Why can't you print a summary of a Sequential model after each add() when no input shape is declared?
questions.answer: Because summary() needs a built model, and without a known input shape the layers have not created their weights.
questions.explanation: The page says you can't print a summary until the model is built.

questions.question: In Listing 7.6, what changes in the summary compared with Listing 7.5, and what stays the same?
questions.answer: The model and layer names change (my_example_model, my_first_layer, my_last_layer); output shapes and parameter counts (256, 650, total 906) stay the same.

questions.answer: build() takes the full input shape including the batch axis, e.g. (None, 3); Input takes the per-sample shape, e.g. (3,).
